'''William Dichtel''' (born 1978, [[Houston, Texas]])<ref name=Northwestern>{{cite web|title=William Dichtel|url=http://www.chemistry.northwestern.edu/people/core-faculty/profiles/william-dichtel.html|website=Dichtel Research Profile|publisher=Northwestern University}}</ref> is an American chemist and the Robert L. Letsinger Professor of Chemistry at [[Northwestern University]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Dichtel Research Group {{!}} At the Interface of Organic and Materials Chemistry|url = http://sites.northwestern.edu/dichtel/|website = Northwestern University}}</ref> He is known for pioneering work in an emerging class of polymers known as [[covalent organic framework]]s (COFs), two-dimensional polymers, and porous materials for [[environmental remediation]] including novel methods for forever chemical (PFAS) destruction and recycling polyurethane foams. Dichtel's research has been recognized nationally and internationally, receiving the [[MacArthur Fellowship]] in 2015, a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 2018,<ref>{{Cite web|title=John Simon Guggenheim Foundation {{!}} Will Dichtel|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/will-dichtel/|access-date=2021-05-23|language=en-US}}</ref> and the Blavatnik National Award in Chemistry in 2020.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://blavatnikawards.org/news/items/blavatnik-national-awards-young-scientists-announce-2020-laureates/ |title=Blavatnik National Awards for Young Scientists Announce 2020 Laureates | publisher = Blavatnik Family Foundation |date = |author = |accessdate= July 22, 2020}}</ref> He also founded Cyclopure, a university spin-off that seeks to bring to market water filtration with [[cyclodextrin]] polymers.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bomgardner|first=Melody M.|date=February 22, 2019|title=CycloPure raises $5 million for cyclodextrin water filtration products|url=https://cen.acs.org/business/start-ups/CycloPure-raises-5-million-cyclodextrin/97/i8|access-date=2021-05-30|website=cen.acs.org}}</ref>

Dichtel is an accomplished marathon open water swimmer. In August 2020, he completed the [https://www.usms.org/fitness-and-training/articles-and-videos/articles/chicago-skyline-swim Chicago Sky Line Swim].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.openwaterswimming.com/professor-will-dichtel-sets-record-overnight-for-chicago-skyline-swim/|title = Professor Will Dichtel Sets Record Overnight For Chicago Skyline Swim}}</ref> He swam the Catalina Channel in July 2022, and the [[English Channel]] on June 25, 2024, in 12 hours, 8 minutes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=William Dichtel - UltraSwimming Database |url=https://ultraswimming.org/database/p/william-dichtel}}</ref> On October 11, 2026, he completed the 20 Bridges Swim around Manhattan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=20 Bridges Swim Around Manhattan Results – New York Open Water |url=https://www.nyopenwater.org/20-bridgesmanhattan-island-swim-solo-swim-results/ |access-date=2026-10-27 |language=en-US}}</ref> These three swims comprise the Triple Crown of Open Water Swimming, which has been completed by approximately 400 individuals as of 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=UltraSwimming Database - Triple Crown |url=https://ultraswimming.org/database/challenges/triple-crown}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Dichtel was born in [[Houston|Houston, Texas]], and raised in [[Roanoke, Virginia]]. He earned a B.S. in Chemistry from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 2000, where he worked with Prof. [[Timothy M. Swager]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=William Dichtel – Dichtel Research Group|url=https://sites.northwestern.edu/dichtel/william-dichtel/|access-date=2021-05-23|website=sites.northwestern.edu}}</ref> He completed his Ph.D. at the University of California, Berkeley in 2005 under [[Jean Fréchet|Jean M. J. Fréchet]], focusing on [[porphyrin]]-containing [[dendrimer]]s for [[Light harvesting materials|light harvesting]] applications.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dichtel|first1=William R.|last2=Serin|first2=Jason M.|last3=Edder|first3=Carine|last4=Fréchet|first4=Jean M. == Independent career ==
Dichtel began his independent career in the Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology at Cornell University in 2008, and was promoted to associate professor in 2014.<ref name=":2" /> He moved to Northwestern University in 2016 as the Robert L. Letsinger Professor of Chemistry. At Northwestern, the Dichtel Research Group focuses on using organic synthesis and noncovalent assembly to control the structure and reactivity of molecules, materials, and interfaces across chemical environments; moreover, the group uses the tools of synthetic chemistry to better understand and design nanostructured materials.

== Research contributions ==
Dichtel’s research integrates synthetic and polymer chemistry to create porous materials and two-dimensional polymers with applications in separations, energy storage, and sustainability.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.chemrev.0c01184|title = Evans, A.M.; Strauss, M.J.; Corcos, A.R.; Hirani, Z.; Ji, W.; Hamachi, L.S.; Aguilar-Enriquez, X.; Chavez, A.D.; Smith, B.J., and Dichtel, W.R. “Two-Dimensional Polymers and Polymerizations.” Chem. Rev. 2022, 122, 442-564. DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemrev.0c01184}}</ref>

'''2D polymers and covalent organic frameworks:''' Dichtel’s research helped establish 2D-COFs as a new class of [[porous polymer]]s,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nchem.695|title = Spitler, E. L.; Dichtel W. R.; “Lewis acid-catalysed formation of two-dimensional phthalocyanine covalent organic frameworks.” Nature Chem. 2010, 2, 672–677.}}</ref> demonstrating redox-active frameworks,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja409421d|title = DeBlase, C. R.; Silberstein, K. E.; Truong, T.; Abruña, H. D.; Dichtel, W. R. “β-Ketoenamine-linked covalent organic frameworks capable of pseudocapacitive energy storage.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2013, 135, 16821–16824. DOI: 10.1021/ja409421d}}</ref> thin-film growth on graphene,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1202747|title = Colson, J. W.; Woll, A. R.; Mukherjee, A.; Levendorf, M. A.; Spitler, E. L.; Shields, V. S.; Spencer, M. A.; Park, J.; Dichtel, W. R.; “Oriented 2D covalent organic framework thin films on single layer graphene.” Science, 2011, 332, 228–231. DOI:10.1126/science.1202747}}</ref> and mechanistic control over crystallization.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jacs.4c04674|title = Natraj, A.; Landman, I. R.; Pelkowski, C. E.; Burke, D. W.; Kewalramani, S.; Dichtel, W. R.; “Nonclassical Crystallization Processes of Single-Crystalline Two-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2024, 146, 16775-16786, DOI: 10.1021/jacs.4c04674}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jacs.2c07166|title = Natraj, A.; Ji, W.; Xin, J.; Catano, I.; Burke, D. W.; Evans, A. M.; Strauss, M. J.; Ateia; M.; Hamachi, L. S.; Gianneschi, N. C.; Alothman, Z. A.; Sun, J.; Yusuf, K.; Dichtel, W. R.; “Single Crystalline Imine-Linked Two -Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks Separate Benzene and Cyclohexane Efficiently.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2022, 144, 19813–19824. DOI: 10.1021/jacs.2c07166}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aar7883|title = Evans, A. M.; Parent, L. R.; Flanders, N. C.; Bisbey, R. P; Vitaku, E.; Chen, L. X.; Gianneschi, N. C.; Dichtel, W. R.; “Seeded Growth of Single-Crystal Two-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks.” Science, 2018, 361, 52–57. DOI: 10.1126/science.aar7883}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja5037868|title = Smith, B. J.; Dichtel, W. R. “Mechanistic studies of two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks rapidly polymerized from initially homogenous conditions.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2014, 136, 8783–8789. DOI: 10.1021/ja5037868}}</ref> In 2025, his team reported the first mechanically interlocked two-dimensional polymer, formed by [[topochemical polymerization]] to yield layered sheets with enhanced mechanical properties.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.ads4968|title = Bardot, M. I.; Weyrich, C. W.; Shi, Z.; Traxler, M.; Stern, C. L.; Cui, J.; Muller, D. A.; Becker, M. L.; Dichtel, W. R. “Mechanically Interlocked Two-Dimensional Polymers.” Science, 2025, 387, 264-269. DOI: 10.1126/science.ads4968}}</ref>

'''Water purification:''' Dichtel developed cyclodextrin-based porous polymers that rapidly remove organic micropollutants<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.201905142|title = Klemes, M. J.; Ling, Y.; Ching, C.; Wu, V.; Helbling, D. E.; Dichtel, W. R. “Reduction of a Tetrafluoroterephthalonitrile‐β‐Cyclodextrin Polymer to Remove Anionic Micropollutants and Perfluorinated Alkyl Substances from Water.” Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2019, 58, 12049-12053. DOI: 10.1002/anie.201905142}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.7b02381|title = Xiao, L.; Ling, Y.; Alsbaiee, A.; Li, C.; Helbing, D. E.; Dichtel, W. R. “β-Cyclodextrin Polymer Network Sequesters Perfluorooctanoic Acid at Environmentally Relevant Concentrations.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2017, 139, 7689-7692. DOI: 10.1021/jacs.7b02381}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doi.org/10.1038/nature16185|title = Alsbaiee, A.; Smith, B. J.; Xiao, L.; Ling, Y.; Helbling, D. E.; Dichtel, W. R. “Rapid removal of organic micropollutants from water by a porous β-cyclodextrin polymer.” Nature, 2016, 529, 190–194. DOI: 10.1038/nature16185}}</ref> and [[PFAS]] from water. These materials underpin commercial products containing DEXSORB® technology from Cyclopure, which he founded in 2016. He also led a 2022 study describing a simple, low-temperature method to degrade multiple PFAS classes using dimethyl sulfoxide and [[sodium hydroxide]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abm8868|title = Brittany Trang et al., Low-temperature mineralization of perfluorocarboxylic acids.Science377,839-845(2022).DOI:10.1126/science.abm8868}}</ref>

'''Recycling thermoset polyurethanes as covalent adaptable networks:''' Dichtel and his research group developed a new recycling method for [[polyurethane foam]]s,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/adma.202305387|title = Kim, S.; Li, K.; Alsbaiee, A.; Brutman, J. P.; Dichtel, W. R. “Circular Reprocessing of Thermoset Polyurethane Foams.” Adv. Mater. 2023, 35, 2305387. DOI: 10.1002/adma.202305387}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c11319|title = Kim, S.; Felsenthal, L. M.; Sala, O.; Welz, O.; Bergeler, M.; Alsbaiee, A.; Dichtel W. R. “Reprocessing Thermoset Polyurethane Foams Using Their Residual Polymerization Catalysts.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2025, 147, 35655-35663. DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5c11319}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscentsci.0c00083|title = Sheppard, D. T.; Jin, K.; Hamachi, L. S; Dean, W.; Fortman, D. J.; Ellison, C. J.; Dichtel, W. R. “Reprocessing Postconsumer Polyurethane Foam Using Carbamate Exchange Catalysis and Twin-Screw Extrusion” ACS Cent. Sci. 2020, 6, 6, 921-927, DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.0c00083}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5b08084|title = Fortman, D. J.; Brutman, J. A.; Cramer, C. J.; Hillmyer, M. A.; Dichtel, W. R. “Mechanically Activated, Catalyst-free Polyhydroxyurethane Vitrimers.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2015, 137, 14019–14022. DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5b08084}}</ref> one of the most common types of plastic, that uses nontoxic, greener catalysts. The process involves chemical reactions that simultaneously reprocess and “refoam” polyurethane after heating in the presence of a catalyst.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscentsci.0c00567|title = Elling, B. R.; Dichtel, W. R. “Reprocessable Cross-Linked Polymer Networks: Are Associative Exchange Mechanisms Desirable?” ACS Cent. Sci. 2020, 6, 1488-1496. DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.0c00567}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5b08084|title = Fortman, D. J.; Brutman, J. A.; Cramer, C. J.; Hillmyer, M. A.; Dichtel, W. R. “Mechanically Activated, Catalyst-free Polyhydroxyurethane Vitrimers.” J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2015, 137, 14019–14022. DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5b08084}}</ref> The types of polymers that require this catalyst approach are called thermosets, or [[cross-link]]ed polymers. Thermosets are important because of their superior durability and stability, but these properties come at the expense of recyclability. New methods to recycle thermosets will reduce [[greenhouse gas emissions]], save energy and decrease landfill use.
